story_text.value:
Hi HN!

One of my favorite apps on macOS, Ice, stopped working when I updated to macOS 27 because the trick it relied on doesn't work anymore. The only thing I really needed from the app was the ability to hide menu bar items to the left of it, so I built Chest to do just that.

There are other apps like this as well that try to use the menu bar part of macOS's exam mode to hide items, but that approach has some issues with the screen sharing, microphone, and camera indicators in the menu bar, which is rather troublesome for me.

Chest works by emulating the "Allow in the Menu Bar" switches in System Settings rather than relying on the old trick of pushing menu bar items off-screen.

It just needs Accessibility permission and access to two files that let it control which items are shown in the menu bar and where they're placed.

You can hide items in two ways: by ⌘-dragging them to the left of a small dot in the menu bar, or by dropping them into a separate "Chest" that keeps them out of the menu bar entirely. Clicking the dot brings the hidden items back.

I think our approach is rather cleaner, and the app itself sits at ~2 MB, so it's small enough to not matter while providing a clutter-free menu bar.

You can view the source at https://github.com/boringbar/chest

title.value: Show HN: Chest – a tiny, open-source menu bar manager for macOS 27

story_text.value:
Ever since January 2025 the Austrian Ministry of Justice has made the Firmenbuch public (and free!) as part of the EUs Open Data Directive.

Firmendaten builds on that: we ingest the filings, extract the balance sheet figures (which, luckily, mostly come as an XML), and make them searchable and comparable across companies and years.

When we set out to do it, it sounded pretty easy: extract the XML, save them in a table, calculate the KPIs and build the from-tend.

However, a few things made it harder than expected.

- Fiscal years don't line up. We compare the latest year both companies filed for. If there is none, each column shows its own latest year and is labelled as such. We also only match on the year, so a balance sheet dated 31 March and one dated 31 December both count as "2024". There's quite some (internal) discussion on how to handle that.

- Small companies don't have to disclose revenue. Small GmbHs/FlexCos file an abridged balance sheet without a P&L, so margins simply aren't available for a large share of companies. Our "growth" figure falls back to total assets, which is a weak signal: it also grows when a company takes on debt. On a more general note: not every financial figure makes equal sense for every industry / company. Ideally, we would have specific numbers, based on the industry.

- Holding companies break ratios. They book dividends from subsidiaries as income on almost no revenue, which gives you profit margins above 100%. That's actually just one part of the issue around holding companies, and subsidies.

- Generated summaries overclaim easily. "Company A is more stably financed" really just means "higher equity ratio". We're still tuning the wording, which is one reason the page is labelled beta. None of the summaries are AI-generated, as that requires quite some tweaking to get right (agin, a lot of the interpretation depends on the industry/company).

story_text.value:
A while back, I needed to make a webhook system for a project I was working on. I pretty quickly found out that webhook auth is not an entirely solved problem with people frequently implementing DIY solutions. I also found out that while using some form of asymmetric signature (eg. oauth tokens) is common with regular api auth, most webhook producers use symmetric signatures (HMAC) instead.

This bugged the hell out of me because the webhook functionality I needed was pretty basic, but using symmetric signatures, which requires the webhook producer to hold onto a secret for every endpoint they send webhooks to, introduced a major secret management problem. Designing and implementing novel secret management techniques for my web app felt like a bad idea, so I started looking into why so many people use symmetric signatures instead of asymmetric signatures.

I frequently saw performance listed as a problem with asymmetric signatures, so I thought this might be why they weren't more broadly used, but a quick benchmark proved that wrong (HMAC signing is much faster, but ed25519 is still fast enough that it doesn't matter).

It seemed like the biggest barrier to using asymmetric signatures was added development complexity. There are small but important details that need to be included in an asymmetric signature, getting asymmetric keys into the right format is more complicated than for symmetric keys, and the crypto libraries you're working with can have sharp edges.

That complexity makes it more difficult for a webhook producer to implement (and document) asymmetric signatures, but then all of their consumers also have to implement the verification step (hopefully correctly). Building a library that does these steps for you is difficult because it has to be available in any language a webhook consumer might be using, not just the language the webhook producer uses.

But it kept bugging me that we're all using a less good form of authentication just because we haven't packaged up the steps to sign and verify an asymmetric signature that is secure for webhooks, so now I've built that library. With a few language implementations to serve as a template, replicating this in enough languages that the large majority of developers can use it feels totally doable, and I am hoping to get several more languages implemented over the next few weeks.

title.value: Show HN: Correct Hooks – Easy webhook auth with asymmetric signatures

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I am a new dad, and as I started paternity leave I had all this time on my hands and started building with Claude.

I built a GitHub contribution chart for my baby’s feeding and one thing led to another. I had a full blown baby tracker in a week. People liked it, the pricing of everything else was obscene so I decided to make it open for other parents with the idea that I keep building it as my baby grows.

We’re not trying to make money, just paying the postgres bill. And it was nice to connect with my wife while building something together, she’s not technical, but she can build!

We also wrote (well, Claude did, my wife keeps saying she wants to rewrite it) our story, and we called the product like our son.

There is a demo page here https://fennimore.milo.baby/demo.

I then hooked it up to an agent for stats, and also automated my Divoom (see https://imgur.com/a/iKat7rD)

We’re entering a phase where software costs nothing to build and nothing to run, and I am ready for the “Parents that code phase of my life”.

title.value: Show HN: A GitHub contribution for my newborn's feedings, turned into SaaS

story_text.value:
pi-cowboy is an agent orchestrator for Pi(https://pi.dev) and Herdr(https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr). Break large jobs into focused subtasks, hand them off to background agents running in parallel, and consolidate the results when they finish. Each agent runs in an isolated copy-on-write Git work-tree, minimising disk overhead.

pi-cowboy can orchestrate foreign harnesses too, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and more.

Feature highlights:

- Foreign harnesses: pi-cowboy agents can run in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pig and Pi-Bolt, as well as Pi. This gives you great flexibility in choosing how to spend your tokens. Running out of Codex usage? Switch your pi-cowboy harness to OpenCode, select one of its free models, and let it handle the rest. Pig and Pi-Bolt are pi variants that are more efficient, with a lower memory footprint and faster performance than pi. Because pi-cowboy is designed to run multiple agents in parallel, having a lower per-agent footprint is crucial. It prevents your machine from running out of resources and lets you have higher concurrency without choking your system.

- Concurrency limits: You can configure concurrency limits at every level. Running a local model with limited resources? If a simple task already takes hours to complete, the last thing you want is to overload your machine by running too many of them at once. Set concurrency limits for that model specifically to keep resource usage under control.

You can install it on Pi as a package:

  pi install npm:pi-cowboy #(requires `herdr` 0.8+)

title.value: Show HN: Pi-cowboy – use Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode as subagents

story_text.value:
I've been working on generative LEGO assembly models recently, but there are similar projects already, so I wanted to try some harder cases: specialized parts (incl. technic), multi-modal prompting (incl. using images, 3D meshes or almost any input), constrained inventory (so you could upload just parts you have), ensuring physical validity and generating buildable instructions, being able to tweak, modify or rebuild entirely an existing build etc.

TL;DR the pipeline got more complex than expected and I ended up with an agentic harness leveraging recursive program synthesis, combinatorial diffusion, semantic 3D search and operations on assembly hypergraphs.

Yet I am quite happy with the result. It should be able to handle as well a functional mechanism, LEGO robot, artistic landscape or fancy animal.

Most importantly, it also checks for subgraph matches of builds present in catalogue, being able to check (and possibly enforce) originality and prevent copying existing MOCs.

Have fun!

story_text.value:
About a year ago I was wondering how hard it'd be to build an e2e enabled emacs matrix client similar to how telega does things: use mature libraries to build a daemon that speaks JSON to emacs.

I did a proof of concept for the e2e bits, and over time built a chat client on top. I recently switched to it as my only client on most devices - and thought maybe it's time to give it a better name than "matrix", and cut it out of my .emacs.d it was developed in. So I asked an LLM to write tests for everything to have a sensible baseline, split it out, and renamed everything.

There probably is still a bit of breakage linking back to my config, but I'm relatively confident all major issues got fixed over the last week of testing.

title.value: Show HN: ElNeo, a E2E enabled matrix client for Emacs, inspired by telega
